newsitem.title: USA: S&P says may cut Hawaii AA GO bond rating.
newsitem.headline: S&P says may cut Hawaii AA GO bond rating.

text.p: Standard & Poor's Corp said Wednesday it placed its AA general obligation (GO) rating on the State of Hawaii's $2.947 billion outstanding GO bonds on CreditWatch with negative implications.
At the same time, Standard & Poor's has assigned its AA rating to Hawaii's $150 million GO bonds of 1996 series CM due 2016.

The CreditWatch placement is based upon Governor Benjamin Cayetano's announcement that he will request the state legislature to authorize an additional $600 million in debt to be issued in fiscals 1998 and 1999.
At over $3,800 per capita, state debt is the second highest of all the U.S. states, after Alaska, and debt servicing consumes nearly 11% of general resources.
If approved by the legislature, the new plan would boost ratios by 20%, although some of the debt is for projects that would have been financed in later years.
The legislature will review the proposal in January 1997 as it deliberates the Governor's biennium budget for fiscals 1998 and 1999.
Ratings will be lowered if these plans are approved.
Additionally, the rating reflects the state's:
-- Concentrated economic base, dominated by a recovering tourism industry;
-- Above-average income levels; and
-- Modest structural budget realignment and a slim financial position.

Hawaii's emergence from a prolonged economic slump is gathering momentum, although employment trends remain weak. Tourism, which is estimated to account for over 23% of Hawaii's gross state product, began a modest recovery in 1994 and has strengthened through the first half of 1996.

The total number of tourists grew a moderate 3.2% in 1995 to 6.6 million visitors, and is up about 6.3% so far for 1996. The average length of stay, however, has declined slightly, dampening the effect of this growth.

Nonagricultural wage and salary employment data suggest that state lost a total of about 10,000 jobs between 1992-1995, and another 2,000 jobs in the first half of 1996, mostly in the construction, manufacturing, and transportation and public utilities sectors.
The Governor's public infrastructure plans are an effort to boost these sectors.
Income levels have declined, but remain above the U.S. average, with per capita personal income at about 111% of the national average.

Although significant structural budgetary realignment has been achieved in the last two years, state finances remain pressed by weakening revenue growth and potentially large increases in labor costs.
The realignment in fiscals 1996 and 1997 followed four years of operating deficits in the $200 million-$300 million range, which were offset though use of reserves and fund equity transfers.

The unreserved general fund balance of nearly $320 million at June 30, 1995 is good at about 10% of current expenditures and transfers, but the result includes $275 million of one-time accruals through the adoption of GASB Statement No. 22.

The state reduced funding for many programs in fiscal 1996, including spending cuts of up to 17% in general government departments, contributing to an improved year-end result of about $161 million on a budgetary basis, up from the $90.3 million reported on that basis in 1995.
The fiscal 1997 performance, however, may be affected by a downward revision of revenues, based on continued softness in construction and the labor market, and potentially costly labor agreements.
Through arbitration, state nurses recently received a wage increase of nearly 6%, which, if extended to other bargaining units, would further weaken the state's position.
The state's financial gains also could be jeopardized by litigation over the allocation of revenues derived from ceded lands, including off-airport duty-free revenues.

The Office of Hawaiian Affairs, representing the interests of native Hawaiians, has received summary judgment at the circuit court level, but the ruling is under appeal with the Hawaiian Supreme Court.
A specific financial claim has not been determined, but it could be well over $100 million, Standard & Poor's said.
--U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650
